body_html:
Colombian slang is warm, polite and very recognizable, thanks in part to music and TV series that travel far beyond Colombia. You will hear parce for a friend, bacano and chévere for anything good, ¿qué más? as a greeting and qué pena as an apology. Colombian Spanish also has a reputation for courtesy: people often ask for things with ¿me regala…? even when paying. Here are the words you will hear most, with notes on the ones that vary by region or can be rude.

Quick answer
  • Friendly and common: parce, bacano, chévere, ¿qué más?, de una
  • Everyday life: tinto (black coffee), guayabo (hangover), plata (money)
  • Very Colombian politeness: qué pena, a la orden, ¿me regala…?
  • Use with care: qué chimba is common in Medellín but has a vulgar origin.
{{toc}}

Colombian slang greetings and reactions

WordMeaningExample
¿Qué más?How are you? What’s up?¡Hola! ¿Qué más? ¿Bien o qué? (Hi! How are you? All good?)
¿Qué hubo? / ¿Quiubo?What’s up?¡Quiubo, parce! (What’s up, buddy!)
de unasure, right away—¿Vamos? —¡De una! (“Shall we go?” “Let’s do it!”)
qué penasorry, excuse me (embarrassed)Qué pena llegar tarde. (Sorry for being late.)
a la ordenat your service, you’re welcome—Gracias. —A la orden. (“Thanks.” “You’re welcome.”)
pailatoo bad, tough luckSe acabó, paila. (It’s sold out, too bad.)
¡Uy, no!Oh no!¡Uy, no, qué tráfico! (Oh no, what traffic!)

Qué pena is a classic misunderstanding. Elsewhere it means “what a pity”, but in Colombia it is a polite apology or a way to get attention: Qué pena, ¿me puede ayudar? (Excuse me, could you help me?).

People, describing things and daily life

WordMeaningExample
parce / parcerobuddy, friendEs mi parcero del colegio. (He’s my buddy from school.)
bacanocool, great¡Qué bacano el plan! (What a great plan!)
chéveregreat, niceLa fiesta estuvo chévere. (The party was great.)
berracotough, brave, amazing (or angry)Ese examen estaba berraco. (That exam was really tough.)
la mamerasomething boring or tiresomeQué mamera hacer fila. (Standing in line is such a drag.)
camellarto work hardToca camellar este fin de semana. (We have to work this weekend.)
la platamoneyNo tengo plata. (I have no money.)
una lucaa thousand pesosCuesta cinco lucas. (It costs five thousand pesos.)
el tintoblack coffee¿Le provoca un tinto? (Would you like a coffee?)
el guayabohangoverTengo un guayabo terrible. (I have a terrible hangover.)
la rumbaparty, going out¿Vamos de rumba? (Shall we go out partying?)

Notice ¿le provoca…?, literally “does it provoke you?”, which Colombians use to mean “would you like…?”. And toca means “we have to” or “it’s time to”: Toca irnos (We have to go).

{{image:2}}

Colombian politeness: ¿me regala…? and usted

Colombians are known for courteous Spanish. In shops and restaurants you will hear ¿Me regala un tinto, por favor?, literally “Will you gift me a coffee?”, which simply means “Can I have a coffee?”. You still pay. Many Colombians also use usted with friends, family and even children, especially in Bogotá and the Andean region, so usted can sound warm rather than distant there.

In Bogotá and Boyacá you may also hear sumercé, an old, very respectful and affectionate form of address. For the general rules, see {{link:tu-vs-usted|tú vs usted}} and {{link:polite-requests-in-spanish|polite requests in Spanish}}.

Words to use with care

  • ¡Qué chimba! means “Awesome!” and is extremely common in Medellín, but the word has a vulgar origin, and chimba can be rude in other contexts. Recognize it; use it only with friends who use it.
  • gonorrea is used as an insult (and sometimes, confusingly, as slang among friends in Medellín). Avoid it.
  • marica can be a friendly filler among young people, but it is also a homophobic slur. Don’t use it.

The Diccionario de americanismos records many of these words with their country labels and register.

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

A sample chat between friends

Vale: ¡Quiubo, parce! ¿Qué más?
What’s up, buddy! How are you?

Andrés: Bien, pero con un guayabo berraco. Anoche fuimos de rumba.
Good, but with a terrible hangover. We went out partying last night.

Vale: Jajaja, paila. ¿Le provoca un tinto?
Haha, tough luck. Want a coffee?

Andrés: ¡De una! Qué pena con usted, siempre me invita.
Sure! Sorry, you always treat me.

Vale: Tranquilo, a la orden.
Don’t worry, my pleasure.

Notice how they use usted with each other even as friends, which is very common in Colombia.

Common mistakes

  • Hearing qué pena as “what a pity”. In Colombia it is usually “sorry” or “excuse me”.
  • Thinking ¿me regala? means free. It is just a polite way to ask; you will still pay.
  • Using Medellín slang in Bogotá formal settings. Parce and qué chimba are casual.
  • Assuming usted is cold. In Colombia it is often warm and respectful.

Compare Colombian words with {{link:mexican-slang|Mexican slang}} and {{link:argentine-slang|Argentine slang}}.

{{image:3}} {{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Colombian slang is friendly and polite at the same time, which makes it a pleasure to learn. Start with ¿qué más?, de una, bacano and qué pena, remember that usted can be warm, and recognize the rude words without using them. For other countries, see my guide to {{link:spanish-slang|Spanish slang}}.

faq.a: It means buddy or friend. It is short for parcero and very common, especially in Medellín.

faq.q: What is the difference between bacano and chévere?
faq.a: Both mean cool or great. Bacano is very Colombian; chévere is also common in Venezuela and other countries.

faq.q: What does “qué pena” mean in Colombia?
faq.a: It is a polite way to say “sorry” or “excuse me”, not “what a pity”.
It is a courteous way to ask for something in shops and restaurants. You still pay.

questions.explain: In Colombia it is a polite apology.
Red wine is vino tinto, but un tinto is coffee.
In Colombian slang it is a hangover.
